750.title: Stoned at Ta'if
750.hook: he walks to Ta'if to seek help, and is mocked and driven out
750.howItsDone: Muslims learn the journey to Ta'if as part of the Meccan sirah, retold just before the night journey, and it is remembered when people face rejection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Talib: the uncle who shielded him died, and the street could reach him. Your line was: the shield is gone.

Mecca has closed its doors. The wife who held him is buried. The uncle who shielded him is buried. So he does something that takes nerve: he leaves, on foot, for Ta'if, a town in the hills, to ask its tribe, Thaqif, for help and a hearing. No army, no escort of clan, no promise of welcome. He's going to knock on the doors of strangers and say what he has said in Mecca. Today: Ta'if.
screen: `MECCA HAS CLOSED.` → `ON FOOT TO THE HILLS.` → `KNOCKING ON STRANGERS' DOORS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says he went to the leaders of Thaqif, three brothers, sat with them and told them why he'd come. Their answers are sharp. One says, in effect, if God sent you, I'll tear the covering of the Ka'ba. Another: couldn't God find anyone but you to send? The third: I won't speak to you at all. If you're really a messenger, you're too great for me to answer, and if you're lying, you're not worth answering. Three doors, shut. He gets up and asks them one thing: then keep this between us. They don't. They stir up the people of the town, and, as the accounts tell it, a crowd follows him out, jeering and shouting, and in some tellings throwing stones, until he reaches an orchard outside town and takes shelter by its wall. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps his own words about a day like this. Years later, Aisha asks whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says the worst was the day of al-Aqabah, when he offered himself to Ibn Abd Yalil and was turned away; commentators connect that day with Ta'if. He went off with his grief, he says, not knowing where he was going, and didn't come to himself until he reached a place called Qarn al-Tha'alib. The man Muslims honor as the final messenger tells his wife that he walked in a daze. The story doesn't hide it. But notice the verb. He went. Hurt and dazed, he kept walking. What he said and met along that road is the next few days.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS, THREE NOS.` · `KEEP THIS BETWEEN US.` · `A CROWD, AND STONES.` · `HE WALKED IN A DAZE.` · then, large: `HE KEPT WALKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one no you've been given lately, a job, an apology not accepted, and let it be as heavy as it is. Then, if you can, take a few slow steps across the room, feeling each foot land, or, if you can't walk right now, press each foot into the floor in turn. You don't have to feel better to take the next step, and if you pray, you can bring that no to Allah as it is.
Ta'if. The hill town where he went for help, was turned away, mocked and driven out, and kept walking. Today's word.
Your line: he walked on. Not healed yet, just walking. Day seven hundred fifty, done.

751.title: The du'a of Ta'if
751.hook: in an orchard outside Ta'if he prays: to You I complain of my weakness; if You are not angry with me, I don't mind (sirah)
751.carry: if you're not angry, I don't mind
751.howItsDone: The du'a of Ta'if is taught in sirah study alongside the journey to Ta'if, and Muslims say its words in times of hardship or rejection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ta'if: three brothers said no, a crowd drove him out, and he kept walking. Your line was: he walked on.

The crowd has fallen back. He's sitting in the shade of a vine, against the wall of an orchard that belongs to two men of Quraysh. Refused by three leaders, jeered at by a town, he has nowhere obvious to go next. What would anyone say, alone, in a moment like that? A complaint about the people of Ta'if would make sense. So would a plea to be avenged. Ibn Ishaq records something else. Today: du'a.
screen: `IN THE SHADE OF A VINE.` → `NOWHERE TO GO.` → `WHAT DOES HE SAY?`

segments.voice: A du'a is a personal prayer, words addressed to Allah in a person's own need, as opposed to the set prayer, the salah. This one, as Ibn Ishaq gives it, begins with a complaint, but not against Thaqif. He complains to Allah of his own weakness: his lack of strength, his lack of means, how small he has become in people's eyes. Then he turns. He calls Allah the most merciful of the merciful, the Lord of the weak, and asks: to whom are You leaving me? To a stranger who will scowl at me, or an enemy given power over me? And then comes today's line. If You are not angry with me, he says, I don't mind. Your well-being, the ease You give, is wider for me. Look at the order. First, honesty: I am weak, I have little, people look down on me. Then a question, almost a child's: who are You handing me to? Only then the turn, which isn't that the pain stops mattering, but that it's measured against one thing. If the relationship with Allah is whole, the rest can be borne. Notice what is missing, too: no curse on Ta'if, no request that the town be punished. That restraint will matter in two days. A note on the source: this du'a comes from the sirah, through Ibn Ishaq, not from Bukhari or Muslim, and hadith scholars have discussed the strength of its chain. Its words are still said today, in hard times.
screen: `A DU'A: A PRAYER IN ONE'S OWN NEED.` · `FIRST: I AM WEAK.` · `TO WHOM ARE YOU LEAVING ME?` · `NO CURSE ON TA'IF.` · then, large: `IF YOU ARE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands open in your lap, and silently name three honest things: where your strength has run low, where you don't have what you need, where you feel small in other people's eyes. If you pray, you can bring them to Allah in your own words, as plainly as he did, or in the words of the du'a of Ta'if if you know them. If you don't pray, notice what it's like to say them without defending yourself.
Du'a, a personal prayer. In an orchard after rejection, he complains to Allah of his own weakness and says: if You are not angry with me, I don't mind. Today's word.
Your line: if you're not angry, I don't mind. Honest about weakness, and still turned toward Allah. That's day seven hundred fifty-one.

752.title: Addas and the grapes
752.hook: a Christian servant from Nineveh brings him grapes and hears him speak of Yunus (sirah)
752.howItsDone: Muslims retell the meeting with Addas as part of the Ta'if story, and say bismillah, in the name of Allah, before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the du'a of Ta'if: honest weakness, and no curse on anyone. Your line was: if you're not angry, I don't mind.
screen: `IF YOU'RE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.`

segments.voice: Two brothers own the orchard where he's resting: Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a, men of Quraysh who are no friends of his message. They've watched what Ta'if did to him, and something in them moves. Ibn Ishaq says they felt for him as a kinsman. They call their servant, a Christian man named Addas: take a bunch of these grapes on a plate to that man, and tell him to eat. Today: Addas.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS WATCH.` → `A PLATE OF GRAPES.` → `CARRIED BY ADDAS.`

segments.voice: Addas sets the grapes down. The Prophet reaches out, and before he eats, he says, in the name of Allah. Addas looks at him. These are not words, he says, that the people of this country say. So the Prophet asks him: where are you from, Addas, and what is your religion? A Christian, Addas says, from Nineveh. And the Prophet answers: from the town of the righteous man Yunus, son of Matta. Addas is astonished. How do you know who Yunus son of Matta was? In Ibn Ishaq's account the Prophet says: he is my brother. He was a prophet, and I am a prophet. And Addas bends over him and kisses his head, his hands and his feet. By the wall, one brother says to the other: well, he's spoiled your servant for you. When Addas comes back they scold him, and he answers that there is nothing on earth better than this man; he told me something only a prophet would know. Look at who meets here. A man just driven out by his own kind. A servant far from home, in a town where nobody says what he says. And between them, a name both of them know: Yunus, whom the Qur'an remembers as one of the messengers, the man of the fish. Christians and Jews tell his story too, as Jonah. What opens the door is not an argument. It's a plate of grapes, two words said before eating, and a question about where someone comes from. And notice who sent the grapes: two men who did not share his faith.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF ALLAH.` · `WHERE ARE YOU FROM, ADDAS?` · `NINEVEH: THE TOWN OF YUNUS.` · `HE IS MY BROTHER.` · then, large: `A BOWL OF GRAPES.`

segments.voice: Think through your week for one person who is running on empty: a coworker on a double shift, a parent with a newborn, someone far from home. Picture something small and real you could bring them, a piece of fruit, a cup of tea, and one question you could ask, the way he asked Addas where he was from. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you next eat.
Addas. A Christian servant from Nineveh who carries grapes to a rejected man, hears him say Allah's name and speak of Yunus, and kisses his hands. Today's word.
Your line: a bowl of grapes. A servant far from home, and a name both men knew. Until tomorrow.

753.title: The angel of the mountains
753.hook: offered the two mountains brought down on his people, he refuses, hoping their children will worship Allah (Bukhari)
753.howItsDone: Muslims retell the angel of the mountains from Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim when speaking of the Prophet's mercy and restraint, and some read it alongside surah 21:107.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Addas: grapes from strangers, and a name both men knew. Your line was: a bowl of grapes.

Revenge, offered from the sky. That's where today's story goes. A few days ago we heard him tell Aisha about the day he was turned away and walked in a daze until he reached Qarn al-Tha'alib. The same report in Sahih al-Bukhari doesn't stop there. When he came to himself, he says, he raised his head, and a cloud was shading him. He looked, and in it was Jibril. Today: the angel of the mountains.
screen: `REVENGE FROM THE SKY.` → `A CLOUD OVERHEAD.` → `JIBRIL IN IT.`

segments.voice: Jibril calls down to him. In Bukhari's report he says, in effect: Allah has heard what your people said to you and how they answered you, and He has sent you the angel of the mountains, to order him as you wish. Then the angel of the mountains himself calls out, greets him, and says: if you wish, I will bring the two Akhshabs together over them. Commentators explain the two Akhshabs as the two mountains on either side of Mecca. Close them, and the people who mocked him are gone. Consider the timing. He has just lost his wife and his uncle. He has been refused, jeered, chased. He's alone. And now he's offered what a wounded person might wish for: the power to make them pay, with heaven's permission. His answer, in Bukhari: No. Rather, I hope that Allah will bring out from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him. Look at what he hoped for. Not that they would apologize, not even that they themselves would change. He looked past the people in front of him to their children and grandchildren, people not yet born. That is a long view, taken on the worst day. It fits the du'a from two days ago, which complained of weakness but cursed no one. Muslims tell this story when they speak of the Prophet as a mercy, and Pickthall's Qur'an puts it this way in surah twenty-one: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples."
screen: `JIBRIL IN THE CLOUD.` · `THE TWO MOUNTAINS CAN CLOSE.` · `NO. I HOPE FOR THEIR CHILDREN.` · `A MERCY FOR THE PEOPLES.` · then, large: `HOPE FOR THEIR CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has hurt you, not the worst person, just someone real, and notice the part of you that would like to see them pay, without scolding it. Then simply decline the revenge for today, which isn't forgiving everything or pretending it didn't happen. Take his long view: wish well to someone connected to them, a child, a friend, a future version of them, and if you pray, ask Allah for good for them.
Jibril. He came with the angel of the mountains' offer to crush the people who had rejected him, and the Prophet refused, hoping for their children instead. Today's word.
Your line: hope for their children. Mercy, chosen on the hardest day. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: By night to Jerusalem
754.hook: he is carried by night from Mecca to the Far Distant Place of Worship, and leads the prophets in prayer (17:1; Muslim)
754.howItsDone: Some Muslim communities remember the Isra and Mi'raj on a night in the month of Rajab, and surah 17 is also called al-Isra after its opening verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the angel of the mountains, and a hope for children not yet born. Your line was: hope for their children.

"Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night." That is how surah seventeen opens in Pickthall's translation, and the surah is known as al-Isra, the night journey. After the losses, after Ta'if, after the cloud and the mountains, the sirah turns to a single night. He is in Mecca, at the sanctuary, on an ordinary night. By morning he will say he has been to Jerusalem and back, and the town will have something new to mock. Today's word: Isra.
screen: `GLORIFIED BE HE WHO CARRIED HIS SERVANT.` → `AFTER THE LOSSES.` → `ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here is the whole opening line in Pickthall: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." The Inviolable Place is the sanctuary at Mecca. The Far Distant Place, in Arabic al-masjid al-aqsa, Muslims understand as the holy place in Jerusalem, and Sahih Muslim names it Bayt al-Maqdis, the House of holiness. Notice the verb: not that he traveled, but that he was carried. Muslim's report from Anas fills in the scene. A white animal called al-Buraq is brought, smaller than a mule and bigger than a donkey, its stride reaching as far as its eye can see. He rides it to Jerusalem, ties it at the ring where the prophets used to tie their mounts, and goes in and prays. Jibril brings him two cups, one of wine and one of milk. He chooses the milk, and Jibril says: you have chosen the fitra, the natural way. Another report in Sahih Muslim adds the detail that gives us today's line. He found himself among a gathering of prophets, and when the time for prayer came, he led them. Picture that row: men whose stories this path has told, standing shoulder to shoulder, and the man just driven out of Ta'if at the front. Muslim scholars have discussed whether the journey was in body and spirit or in a vision, and the sources record that discussion. What the tellings share is the night, the distance, and the row.

755.title: Through the heavens
755.hook: he rises through the heavens, meeting Adam, Isa, Yahya, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa and Ibrahim (Bukhari)
755.howItsDone: Muslims learn the order of the heavens and the prophets met in each from the hadith of the Mi'raj, and say 'peace be upon him' after a prophet's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isra: carried by night to Jerusalem, at the front of a row of prophets. Your line was: the prophets in one row.

A gate in the sky, and a voice behind it asking: who is it? Jibril. And who is with you? Muhammad. Has he been sent for? Yes. Then welcome to him; what an excellent visit. And the gate opens. In Sahih al-Bukhari, that short exchange happens again and again, at gate after gate. Muslims tell it as the same night as yesterday's journey: Jerusalem was the first leg. Now he rises. Today's word: Mi'raj, the ascent.
screen: `WHO IS IT?` → `HAS HE BEEN SENT FOR?` → `THE GATE OPENS.`

segments.voice: Mi'raj is the name Muslims give to the ascent. Bukhari's reports, from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a and others, walk through it heaven by heaven, and at each one, someone is waiting. In the first heaven, Adam. Another report in Bukhari, from Abu Dharr, describes figures to his right and to his left: when he looks to the right he laughs, and when he looks to the left he weeps. They are his own descendants, the people of the garden on one side, the people of the fire on the other. In the second heaven, two cousins, Yahya and Isa, John and Jesus. In the third, Yusuf. In the fourth, Idris. In the fifth, Harun, the brother of Musa. In the sixth, Musa himself. And in the seventh, Ibrahim. At each heaven the greeting is nearly the same. Adam and Ibrahim say: welcome, righteous son, righteous prophet. The others say: welcome, righteous brother, righteous prophet. Son, from the fathers. Brother, from the rest. A few days ago, three brothers in Ta'if wouldn't even speak to him. Now every heaven has family in it. Beyond the seventh heaven, the reports describe the lote tree of the furthest boundary, which the Qur'an mentions in surah fifty-three. The Qur'an itself gives few details of the ascent; the details are in the hadith. Some of these names appear in the Bible too, as Adam, John, Jesus, Joseph, Aaron, Moses and Abraham. Here they stand at their stations, waiting to say welcome.

756.howItsDone: Muslims pray the five daily prayers, salah, at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night, and the story of how fifty became five is taught with the Mi'raj.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mi'raj: welcomed at every heaven, as a son or as a brother. Your line was: met at every heaven.

Of everything that happened on the night of the ascent, what he carried home for his community to keep was a daily practice. And according to Sahih al-Bukhari, it started out much bigger than the one Muslims keep today, and it changed size because of a conversation with Musa on the way down. Today closes our week of sorrow and wonder: from Ta'if to the heavens, and back to the prayer mat. Fifty become five.
screen: `HE CARRIED HOME A PRACTICE.` → `IT STARTED BIGGER.` → `MUSA ON THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Bukhari keeps it in reports from Abu Dharr and from Malik ibn Sa'sa'a. At the highest point of the ascent, Allah enjoins on him and his community fifty prayers a day. He accepts and starts back down. He passes Musa, in the sixth heaven, and Musa asks: what were you commanded? Fifty prayers. And Musa, the prophet who led a whole people out of Egypt and through the wilderness, speaks from experience. In Bukhari's words, roughly: your community won't be able to bear it. I have dealt with people before you. Go back and ask your Lord to lighten it. So he goes back, and it is lightened. Down again past Musa, and Musa says the same thing: go back. Back and forth, the reports say, until it is five. And Musa says, still too much, go back once more. Here the Prophet says something very human: I have asked my Lord until I feel ashamed. I am content, and I accept. Then the word comes: they are five, and they are fifty. My word does not change. So the number got smaller, and the weight didn't. Look at who helped. Not an angel, but Musa, an older prophet who had led a difficult people and knew what daily life does to good intentions. And look at the week behind us: a man refused at Ta'if, comforted with grapes, offered revenge and refusing it, carried to Jerusalem, welcomed at every heaven. What he brings back down is five times a day.
